poems:
6:00 p.m., and the onions go in.
The house agrees to be a house.
Somebody's timer goes off for something nobody set it for.

Garlic hits the butter.
The smell gets there first.

A boy has been called twice.
The third call will use his middle name.
The dishwasher, still full of clean plates from yesterday, is asked to solve this.
Steam on the inside of the kitchen window.

Someone in the next apartment is chopping on a plastic board.
The rhythm is not good, but it is steady.
Wooden spoon across the pot rim, handle up, one drip forming.

INGREDIENTS
onion
ground beef
whatever was in the door of the fridge
salt
more salt
The news is on but nobody has looked at it since the weather.
6:10 p.m. A car door in the driveway. The dog knows whose.
Two burners going, and one forgotten pot of water that will boil in a minute and be needed in twelve.

Hold the knife like this.
Curl your fingers under.
No, under.
That's it.

Rice: a grain that requires you
to leave it alone. Nobody can.
Someone stands in the refrigerator light, learning nothing.
6:15 p.m. Halfway to the table.

A hand reaches past another hand for the salt without a word being needed.
Twenty years of that.
The chicken has ten more minutes. Everyone has been told. Everyone will ask again at 6:22.
Oil pops. Someone says a word they do not say in front of the kids.
Carrot peel curled against the sink, still orange.

6:20 p.m. The table set by a child,
forks on a diagonal, perfect.
A pan of onions past translucent, edging brown at the outside.

How was your day.
Fine.
That's it, fine?
Fine, Dad.
Somewhere a shift is starting, the badge scanned, the coat hung, the first cart pushed.
The tea towel over the shoulder gets used nine times in an hour.

Three pans,
one back burner,
and a plan that was never written down.
In some kitchen the smoke alarm will be the timer. It will not be this one, probably.
Nobody has set the table. This is discovered at 6:27, as it is every day.
A jar of something opened in June, sniffed, kept.
The bus that runs every twenty minutes lets one more person off two blocks from here.
The lid goes on and the arguing stops for exactly as long as the lid stays on.

Butter.
Foil.
Half a lemon.
An elastic band.
The counter as it actually is.

The math worksheet has soup on it now.
Everyone agrees this changes things.
Exhaust fan, middle setting, half the job.
A phone rings in another room and everyone decides it is not theirs.

The pan does not consult the sky.
Onions first, same as anywhere.
Wine poured into the sauce, then a smaller amount into a glass.
The second parent is in traffic and has texted an emoji of a car.
A knife, a cutting board, a small hill of parsley stems pushed to the corner.
The oven light is on. It is what everyone is looking at.
Feed the cat before it becomes a subject.
Someone eats standing up over the sink and does not count it as dinner.
The radio host, still on the same road closure, has said it four times.
Grease on the front of a shirt that was fine all day.

Bring it.
Bring the whole thing.
No, the whole thing.
6:45 p.m. Two more minutes. It has been two more minutes for a while.
The dog is stationed where the food is most likely to fall, and is correct.
In a house with nobody in it, one bowl in the rack, drying.
A cold takeout container, three days old, held up and offered to the room. No takers.

The pot boils over.
The hiss on the burner.
Somebody moves fast in socks.
6:50 p.m. Plates down, two forks short.
A microwave counts down for one person who has already left the room.
More salt than the recipe wanted. Again.
The blue chair scrapes. The old dog stands up because everyone else did.
Grace, if it happens, is short.

First bite.
Nobody talks.
That is the review.
One of them says the thing they have been holding since the car.
Ketchup on a good meal. Let it go.
Someone else's dinner smells better through a screen door on the ground floor.
6:59 p.m. The pan is empty. Nobody has moved yet.
